catalog_citation: Grant, William & Dixon, James Main. 1921. Manual of Modern Scots. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. Part I (Phonology).
catalog_locator: sec. 216 'Stress', p. 62 (archive.org manualofmodernsc00granuoft djvu text); contrast sec. 217 'Words in the breath group', p. 63
catalog_quote: 216. Stress is the comparative force of the breath current, with which the syllables that make up a word are uttered. In Sc. and E. the root syllable of native words is generally the one that has the chief stress. As this root syllable is very often the first in the word, there is a tendency to stress foreign words in the first syllable. In Sc. we often find Romance words retaining their original stress contrary to English usage, e.g. April a'prail consequence konsa'kwens discord dis'kord massacre ma'sakar mischief mis'tfif novel no'vel soiree sa'ri:. On the other hand we have dispute (sb.) 'dispjut police 'polis.

audit.recode_to: No class change. Set caution = "Source states the rule jointly for Scots and English ('In Sc. and E. the root syllable of native words is generally the one that has the chief stress'); Wilson 1915 p. 57 and Dieth 1932 sec. 92 p. 78 likewise say Scots words are stressed as in (Standard) English apart from a listed set of Romance loans (April, July, mattress, mischief, discord, massacre, soiree, novel; police/dispute with earlier stress). Class differs from stan1293 ('weight-hedged', Hayes 1982) by analytical frame (1921 descriptive root-stress vs 1982 generative weight analysis of Latinate vocabulary), not by a described difference between the languages." Add Wilson 1915 p. 57 and Dieth 1932 sec. 92 pp. 78-79 to sources as open corroboration. Any harmonization is a decision on stan1293 or catalog policy, not a reclassify of this record: no Scots source describes weight sensitivity, so reclassification Scots to 'weight-hedged' would be unsourced.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: sec. 216 found verbatim in the held archive.org djvu text (lines 5979-6025); printed page confirmed as p. 62 via archive.org BookReader leaf map (leaf 86 = p. 62); sec. 217 follows as stated. (2) Deciding source: Grant & Dixon 1921 is Glottolog's top-ranked grammar for Scots (xxii+500 pp), its phonology written by a professional phonetician; it is old but first-hand and remains the only full descriptive grammar of general Modern Scots with a phonology part. Four open primary descriptions downloaded now (Wilson 1915 p. 57; Grant 1931 SND Intro sec. 28; Dieth 1932 sec. 92 p. 78; Murray 1873) independently confirm the content: Germanic root/initial stress as in English, with a recurring listed set of Romance loans keeping non-English (later) stress and a few with earlier stress (police, dispute). Macafee & Aitken 2002 adds the Older Scots history of the same loan-stress split.

sources.quote: Historical (Older Scots) only: French loans cited 'with retained stress' on final syllables (baroun, cullour, jelous) beside later 'shift of stress to the first syllable in such words as argu, vertu'; OSL operating on 'antepenultimate open syllables with fronted stress' in mots savants (minister/meinister). No synchronic Modern Scots stress rule.

sources.citation: Dieth, Eugen. 1932. A Grammar of the Buchan Dialect (Aberdeenshire), Descriptive and Historical. Vol. I: Phonology - Accidence. Cambridge: Heffer. (Glottolog 570557, 213 pp, listed by Glottolog as a phonology)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Words of two or more syllables are stressed, in principle, as in StE. Obvious exceptions are: ma'tras "mattress", e'prail "April", mis'tSif "mischief"; stra'veg ... It is the Germanic way of stressing, whereby the main stress is put on the radical, i.e. generally the first syllable. But in Buchan speech the relative weight of root and ending is not the same as, e.g., in StE., Northern G. or Icelandic. The first syllable predominates little, the second is heavy; disyllables are almost pronounced with level stress.' Footnote: French-loan prefixes 'cannot have had much stress', hence aphetic for

sources.quote: 'Stress - i.e. the relative force of the breath current - plays an important part in the modification of sounds ... sec. 28.2. Sometimes the stress shifts in a word, leading to a change in vowel or consonant - e.g. 'un'cuth became 'uncuth and then 'unco; Eng. po'lice, Sc. 'pollis; so also gutcher (grandfather) for gude'sire, 'cummer (gossip) for com'mere. sec. 28.3. Words of small importance in a sentence are slightly stressed and their elements change in quality.' No general placement rule beyond this; consistent with G&D sec. 216-217.
